summary:
Indonesia is a high-risk destination for trans visitors. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, this provision effectively criminalises all consensual same-sex relations; reporting indicates that prosecutions are selective rather than systematic.

Two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women alongside national morality provisions. In Aceh, where Sharia law applies, two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025, and those punishments reach anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors. Enforcement elsewhere takes the form of venue raids: on 22 June 2025 Indonesian police raided a privately rented villa after public reports of a "gay party" and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman, an operation Amnesty International's Deputy Director Wirya Adiwena called a blatant violation of human rights and privacy, noting that the gathering violated no law.

There is a directly documented death of a trans traveller in Indonesian custody. Rodrigo Ventocilla Ventosilla, a Harvard student and trans activist from Peru, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges while on honeymoon in 2022. During a WhatsApp call his mother in Lima was told that authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody; his mother alleges police beat him, while Indonesian police deny that violence was used.

Official policy now frames LGBTQ+ people as a security matter. A presidential decree issued by President Prabowo Subianto in October 2025 lists nonmilitary threats and places LGBTQ+ people within national defence policy as risks to be monitored and controlled. Reporting from August 2026 ties that framing to a wave of vigilante attacks on transgender women; commentators quoted by ABC News state that the regulation moved hostile rhetoric into the official doctrine of national defence policy.

Lampung stands under this national framework. OutRight International's Creeping Criminalisation study names Lampung among eight Indonesian provinces — Aceh, DKI Jakarta, East Kalimantan, North Sumatera, South Sulawesi, South Sumatera and Yogyakarta alongside it — whose regional regulations discriminate against LGBT people, analysed at both province and district level.

The principal Lampung-specific incident in the sources is a November 2018 operation in which Satpol PP, the regional morals-and-order force, raided three transwomen, detained them at the Satpol PP office and hosed them down at the firefighter building while an officer recorded the act. A UNSW human-rights review of violence against transgender women classifies the episode as police-perpetrated violence.

For a visitor, the exposure in Lampung is documented police contact escalating into recorded humiliation and violence, set against a national environment in which an official decree treats LGBTQ+ people as a security risk and vigilante attacks on trans women are reported. The sources assembled for this province do not support a patterned, continuous campaign of enforcement against visitors in Lampung itself.
tangentialFactors:
The UNSW review situates the Lampung raid within a national pattern: transgender women were murdered in 2017 in Bone, Semarang and South Sulawesi, and lobbying for anti-LGBT regional bylaws has run through election cycles from 2016 onward.

Public hostility is measurable. An SMRC survey of 1,520 Indonesians conducted in November 2016 found that 16.6% of respondents hated LGBT people.

OutRight International's finding places Lampung in a group of eight provinces with discriminatory regional regulation, so the legal exposure is not unique to this province; Aceh stands apart within that group because its punishments are imposed under provincial religious law and apply to anyone physically present.

The national decree of October 2025 and the reported surge of mob attacks on transgender women in August 2026 supply the background against which a visitor's police or public contact in Lampung would be interpreted.
localsOnly:
Residents of Lampung live under regional regulations that OutRight International identifies as discriminatory toward LGBT people at both province and district level, and these rules are enforced domestically by Satpol PP, a provincial morals-and-order force with power to raid, detain and humiliate people it targets.

The November 2018 raid was carried out by that domestic force rather than by an agency processing travellers, and the detention and hosing of the three transwomen took place at official facilities, with an officer filming the treatment.

Residents also operate under the national penal code provisions in force since 2 January 2026 and under the October 2025 presidential decree that treats LGBTQ+ people as a monitored security risk, a framing associated with vigilante attacks reported in August 2026.

Local political organising has included election-cycle lobbying for anti-LGBT bylaws since 2016, and survey evidence from November 2016 recorded open hostility toward LGBT people among a substantial minority of the population.
outOfScopeNotes:
The specific text, penalties and current status of any Lampung bylaw that OutRight International names as discriminatory are not stated in the sources available here; only the province's inclusion in the eight-province analysis is established.

Whether any officer involved in the November 2018 raid faced disciplinary or criminal proceedings is unresolved and not sourced.

No Lampung-specific incidents, arrests or newly enacted local bylaws after November 2018 are recorded in the material assembled for this province, and the material contains no visitor-facing documents, border-screening procedures or identity-document rules for Lampung.

It is not sourced whether the national enforcement trends reported for 2025 and 2026 — villa raids, the penal code provisions, the presidential decree — have produced prosecutions or raids within Lampung specifically.
